expectations.text: Rejects cutting every tenant's cap to 4,000 req/min as the fix
expectations.evidence: 'Recommendation: don't cut everyone to 4,000 req/min.'

expectations.text: Identifies the incident as the canonical noisy-neighbor case where the caller stays under its own cap, so tighter per-tenant request caps alone cannot fix it
expectations.evidence: 'The 2am pain is shared-resource contention... 4,000 heavy requests a minute can still saturate the backend.'

expectations.text: Applies a tenant-level ceiling as the first fairness layer, where the tier table applies
expectations.evidence: '1. Tenant ceiling. The 10,000/min cap stays.'

expectations.text: Applies per-user limits inside the tenant's allocation as the second layer, addressing the 40-seat shared org key so one seat cannot spend the whole tenant budget
expectations.evidence: 'Per-identity limit. This fixes the 40-seat problem.'

expectations.text: Applies a per-endpoint-class carve-out as the third layer, isolating the expensive export operations from the general budget
expectations.evidence: 'Bulk class carve-out with concurrency cap.'

expectations.text: Proposes weighted sharing (per-tenant weights with capacity divided proportionally) instead of a hard per-tenant cliff, so a small tenant is never starved to zero
expectations.evidence: 'Divide it by tier weight, with Deficit Round Robin... so a small tenant is never starved to zero.'

expectations.text: Names the weighted-sharing trade: a deterministic guaranteed rate is given up to eliminate the fully-blocked-small-tenant cliff
expectations.evidence: The trade-off is never stated.

expectations.text: Adds a concurrency limiter for the expensive endpoints, not only a requests-per-window number
expectations.evidence: 'Bulk concurrency 8 in-flight'.

expectations.text: Presents defense-in-depth with multiple simultaneous limiter types as the mature end state rather than picking one mechanism
expectations.evidence: Org ceiling, per-identity, bulk class, concurrency, weighted sharing and load shedding are layered.

expectations.text: Distinguishes load shedding from rate limiting (it keys off overall system state, so a well-behaved tenant can still be shed) and requires the published policy to disclose this rather than overclaim fairness
expectations.evidence: 'even a tenant within its quota can see a 429... A fairness promise that omits it overclaims.'

expectations.text: Keeps internal fairness machinery (weights, deficit round robin, shedders) out of the published policy, documenting only externally observable effects
expectations.evidence: 'This is internal architecture. Publish only what callers can observe.'

expectations.text: Acknowledges the quota paradox knowingly: throttling reduces the throttled tenant's own availability even when spare capacity existed, and this is an accepted trade, not a hidden one
expectations.evidence: Work-conserving elasticity 'avoids the paradox'. It is treated as something to avoid, not an acknowledged trade that is accepted.
